intro: Twelve of Krakow's protected trees stand within a few streets of Planty, the park ring where the medieval walls came down, splitting into two short walks: one runs past the ring's biggest plane and ginkgo to a pair of ash trees, the other from a tree of heaven on ul. Swietego Jana to an oak and ginkgo sharing a street on ul. Batorego. Three more grow in Poland's oldest botanical garden, a short walk east. The oldest of all sits six kilometres south, saved by one neighbour.
meta_description: Krakow's most remarkable trees: two short walks around the Planty park ring, three in Poland's oldest botanical garden, and the roadside Henryk Oak.
question_answer: Krakow's oldest tree is the Henryk Oak in Borek Falecki, roughly 240 to 250 years old, beside ul. Zakopianska about six kilometres south of the Old Town. It is named after Henryk Bartyzel, the neighbour who kept it from being felled for most of the 20th century. That crown rests on the best evidence anyone has rather than on a settled measurement: the ages of the big protected trees on the Planty ring are calculated from trunk girth rather than read from records, and on girth alone the plane by the Philharmonic could be older.
question_meta: The Henryk Oak in Borek Falecki, roughly 240 to 250 years old, is Krakow's oldest tree, named for the neighbour who spent decades protecting it.
question_context: The Henryk Oak is the last living fragment of a pine-and-oak forest that once covered the village of Borek, on Krakow's southern edge, the same wood that gave the settlement its name, bor being an old Polish word for pine forest. It became a roadside tree in 1790, not long after Poland's first partition, when Austrian authorities drove the new highway from Vienna to Lwow through the old stand. For most of the 20th century one man kept it standing: Henryk Bartyzel lived beside the tree from 1923 until 2010, intervening when occupation authorities ordered it felled during the Second World War and again through decades of routine road works. A civic council named the tree in his honour the year he died, in 2017 more than 90 volunteers restored the ground around its base, and the following year it went into Poland's national Tree of the Year contest. One caveat belongs with the ranking. This oak is among the few trees in the city anyone has put a number on. The protected veterans on the Planty ring carry ages worked out from trunk girth, and two of them have no age at all.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Krakow?
faq.a: The Henryk Oak in the Borek Falecki district, roughly 240 to 250 years old, named for Henryk Bartyzel, the neighbour who protected it for decades. It holds the title partly because it is one of the few Krakow trees anyone has actually dated.

faq.q: Can you see Krakow's protected trees in one walk?
faq.a: Most of them, in two short walks rather than one. One runs about 1.8 kilometres from the plane on ul. Studencka along the Planty ring, past its biggest plane and ginkgo, to the ash trees on ul. Straszewskiego, Plac Kossaka and ul. Tarlowska. The other, about 1.4 kilometres, runs from the tree of heaven on ul. Swietego Jana past the Turkish hazel and the lime on ul. Krowoderska to the columnar oak on Skwer Bartoszewskiego and the oak and ginkgo on ul. Batorego. All twelve of those trees are free and open at any hour. Three more grow in the Jagiellonian University's Botanical Garden, a short walk from either route, which charges a modest entry fee. The Henryk Oak is the outlier, six kilometres south in Borek Falecki, reachable by tram.

faq.q: How old is the Jagiellonian Oak really?
faq.a: Around 230 years, not the 500 popularly claimed for years. A dendrochronological study corrected the figure, making it roughly as old as the Botanical Garden itself, founded in 1783.

faq.q: Where is Poland's oldest black locust tree?
faq.a: In the Jagiellonian University's Botanical Garden, in front of Collegium Sniadeckiego on the Kopernika Street side: 239 years old by a 2022 measurement, with a trunk 475cm around.

trees.name: The Jagiellonian Oak

location.address: Botanical Garden of the Jagiellonian University, ul. Kopernika 27, Krakow

trees.story: For generations, guides at Poland's oldest botanical garden told visitors this oak was 500 years old, older than the university faculty that planted the garden around it. A dendrochronological study eventually corrected the number to roughly 230, a reminder that even a garden built by scientists can carry a folk legend for two centuries before anyone tests it properly. The real number is less dramatic but not much less impressive: the tree is very nearly as old as the garden itself, founded in 1783 when the Commission of National Education bought monastic land from the Jesuits to give the Krakow Academy's chemistry and natural history faculty somewhere to grow a teaching collection. Sitting at the heart of that collection ever since, the Jagiellonian Oak has outlived the partitions of Poland, two world wars, and the garden's own repeated redesigns. Its species is the single most common one Krakow protects today, a pedunculate oak among 121 individual specimens registered across the city as of 2023, but this particular tree is the one the garden itself calls its most impressive, trunk now six metres around. It stands for anyone who buys the garden's modest entry ticket, its crown wide enough to shade a good stretch of the main path, still growing quietly while its age keeps getting revised downward by better science.
trees.access: Paid entry, Jagiellonian University Botanical Garden (open seasonally, check hours)
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk (garden is close to the Old Town's eastern edge)
trees.notes: Age correction (folk estimate of 500 years versus dendrochronological finding of roughly 230) confirmed by the Botanical Garden's own official page and repeated in Polish Wikipedia's entry on the garden. Coordinates are the garden's general address point, not a surveyed position for the specific tree within the 9.6-hectare grounds.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Henryk Oak

location.address: Near ul. Zakopianska, Borek Falecki, Krakow

trees.story: This oak is named after the man who spent decades making sure it did not get cut down, not after anyone who planted it. Henryk Bartyzel, who lived beside the tree from 1923 until his death in 2010, is the reason it survived a felling order from wartime occupation authorities and decades of routine maintenance on what became one of Krakow's busiest streets. The oak itself predates him by more than a century: it is the last survivor of the pine-and-oak forest that once covered the former village of Borek, the same wood that gave the village its name, bor being an old Polish word for pine forest, and it became a roadside tree almost by accident in 1790, when Austrian authorities cut the Vienna-to-Lwow highway straight through the ancient stand shortly after Poland's first partition. Everything else that forest once held is gone; only this oak, now around 240 to 250 years past that road-building, is left standing at its edge. In 2010, a civic council formally named it Henryk in Bartyzel's honour, and in 2017 a community restoration project reopened its surroundings after more than 90 volunteers cleared and replanted the ground around its base. It competed, as Krakow's first entrant, in Poland's national Tree of the Year contest in 2018.
trees.access: Free, open access, roadside on public ground in Borek Falecki
trees.transport: Borek Falecki tram loop (Zakopianska), short walk
trees.notes: History (1790 road-cutting, Bartyzel's protection from 1923-2010, 2010 naming, 2017 community restoration, 2018 Tree of the Year entry) confirmed across the official Krakow senior-citizens news page and a Nasze Miasto Krakow local news article giving the '240-year-old' figure; the age range here (240-250) allows for the years since that undated article. Exact coordinates are Zakopianska street's general area (Nominatim-geocoded), not a surveyed point for the specific tree, which sources place near a former bus depot on that street without a precise address.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: Poland's Oldest Black Locust

location.address: In front of Collegium Sniadeckiego, Botanical Garden of the Jagiellonian University, ul. Kopernika side, Krakow

trees.story: Black locusts are not supposed to be rare in Poland. The species arrived from North America in the 18th century and spread so successfully across Central Europe's sandy soils that it now grows practically everywhere, valued for holding loose ground rather than for looking distinguished. Which is what makes the specimen standing in front of Collegium Sniadeckiego, on the Kopernika Street side of the Jagiellonian University's Botanical Garden, worth singling out: at 239 years old by a 2022 measurement, with a trunk 475cm around and a height of 27 metres, it is the oldest confirmed black locust anywhere in Poland. Its age lines up almost exactly with the garden's own founding in 1783, meaning whoever first planted it did so within a few years of the garden's earliest plantings, one of the collection's original survivors rather than a later addition. May brings the reward for anyone who times a visit right: a black locust in full bloom carries heavy clusters of white flowers that draw bees from across the garden, the same nectar that makes the species one of Europe's most productive honey trees. It shares this stretch of path with a run of other exceptionally old specimens dating to the same founding decades, giving one corner of the garden a disproportionate share of Poland's oldest confirmed trees.
trees.access: Paid entry, Jagiellonian University Botanical Garden (open seasonally, check hours)
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk
trees.notes: The 'oldest confirmed black locust in Poland' claim, the 2022 measurements (239 years, 475cm circumference, 27m height) and the founding-era planting date are given directly by the Botanical Garden's own official page and repeated in a Gazeta Krakowska feature marking the garden's 240th anniversary in 2023; both agree without contradiction.

best_time.label: May, when it flowers in heavy white clusters

trees.name: The Sniadecki Dogwoods

location.address: Main path, Botanical Garden of the Jagiellonian University, ul. Kopernika 27, Krakow

trees.story: Jan Sniadecki was one of the Enlightenment's great Polish polymaths, an astronomer and mathematician who reformed how Krakow's university taught science, and tradition credits him with personally planting these cornelian cherries along the Botanical Garden's main path around 1790, while he was directing the observatory next door. Cornelian cherry is usually grown as a large shrub rather than what most people picture as a tree, which is part of why these specimens stand out: at roughly 230 years old, they are among the oldest cultivated cornelian cherries recorded in Poland, multi-stemmed and gnarled in a way that reads more like an old apple tree than the tidy hedge shrub gardeners plant today. They flower before almost anything else in the garden wakes up, small clusters of yellow blossom opening as early as February while frost is still a real possibility, followed by tart red fruit in late summer that Polish households have turned into preserves and liqueur for centuries. Sniadecki's connection to the garden runs deeper than one planting: the university's astronomical observatory, which he helped establish, still stands in the Collegium building the garden surrounds, and the dogwoods are the closest thing to a living monument to the man himself, unlabelled and easy to walk past without knowing what they are.
trees.access: Paid entry, Jagiellonian University Botanical Garden (open seasonally, check hours)
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk
trees.notes: Only one source found (the Botanical Garden's own 'oldest specimens' page), which itself presents the Sniadecki planting as tradition ('according to tradition') rather than documented fact; the age (c.1790, roughly 230 years) is the garden's own figure. Flagged for single-source attribution on the planting story specifically, though the trees' existence, species, and age are not in dispute.

best_time.label: February and March, when it flowers before its leaves appear

trees.name: The Filharmonia Plane
trees.age_estimate: estimated 150 to 270 years, from its girth

location.address: Planty Krakowskie, near the Krakow Philharmonic (ul. Zwierzyniecka side), Krakow

trees.story:
Krakow protects ten London planes on the Planty ring, and this is the one that dwarfs the other nine. Its trunk measures 520 centimetres around, comfortably the largest girth in that group, which is what earned it a place on the city's natural monument register in 1997. Nobody has dated it. What exists is the girth, and running that figure through a published growth-factor method puts the tree somewhere between 150 and 270 years old. The band is deliberately wide. The calculation borrows its growth rate from a related American species because no factor for the London plane was found, and a tree standing in a city grows at a speed no formula can know. Read the number as an estimate taken off the trunk rather than a birth year.

The park underneath is better documented than the tree in it. Planty was laid out in the 1820s, after Krakow pulled down its medieval walls and ringed the Old Town with gardens instead. Nothing records when this plane went into that ground. Nor is the register any guarantee of survival: two other protected trees in the same part of the city, a red beech by the Archaeological Museum and a horse chestnut on ul. Podzamcze, were brought down by storms in February 2022 and July 2021.
trees.access: Free, public park (Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Krakow Glowny railway station or Filharmonia tram/bus stops, short walk through Planty
trees.notes: Girth 520cm and the 1997 designation come from Krakow's own natural monument registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against the independent GDOS/CRFOP register entry (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.1111, gid 72032). The age is DERIVED from girth using a published growth factor borrowed from American sycamore, the closest documented proxy for London plane; the 150-270 band reflects that proxy plus urban growing conditions and is not to be narrowed without a dendrochronological source. Largest girth of the ten protected London planes on the Planty ring.

trees.name: The Straszewskiego Ash
trees.age_estimate: estimated 150 to 220 years, from its girth

location.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto (Planty ring, west side near Wawel)

trees.story:
European ash is one of the commonest trees in Poland and a thick one is not common at all. This specimen stands on the pavement of ul. Straszewskiego, on the western edge of Planty a few minutes below Wawel, and measures 375 centimetres around. That is what earned it a place on the city's natural monument register in 1987.

Its age is arithmetic rather than record. The girth works out at roughly 119 centimetres of diameter, and a published growth factor returns something near 190 years from that. Two things keep it a range instead of a number. The factor is borrowed from green ash, the closest documented relative that has one, and no tape measure can see what two centuries of drought years, good years and street rebuilding did inside the trunk. Call it 150 to 220 years and leave it there. Only a core sample would settle it.

The species itself has had a hard three decades. A fungal dieback spreading west since the 1990s has thinned ash across Europe, killing young and old trees alike and making veterans of this size less ordinary every year than they used to be. This one is still standing, on a public pavement, free to walk up to at any hour.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Straszewskiego, bordering Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Wawel tram/bus stops or Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk
trees.notes: Girth 375cm and the 1987 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.892, gid 72079). Age DERIVED from girth with the published growth factor for green ash, the closest documented proxy in the same genus; 150-220 band, not to be narrowed without a dendrochronological source.

trees.name: The Garncarska Ginkgo
trees.story:
Three trunks rise from a single base on ul. Garncarska, and the number the register carries, 275 centimetres, belongs to the largest of them rather than to one trunk. The other two measure 203 and 175. Krakow listed the tree as a natural monument in 1968, decades earlier than most of the entries around it, which suggests somebody thought it unusual long before the modern register caught up.

How old is it? Nobody knows, and here guessing would be worse than saying so. The girth-to-age arithmetic that dates the oaks and limes on this walk needs a growth factor calibrated to the species, and no reliable one exists for ginkgo: the tree thickens at wildly different rates depending on cultivar, site and how much room its roots were given. So the age field stays empty on purpose. If you have seen a planting record for this stretch of Garncarska, or a photograph old enough to help, tell us.

What it does reliably deliver is November. Ginkgo leaves turn from green to a flat butter gold and then let go almost all at once, often within a couple of days, which on a three-stemmed tree of this size means a great deal of gold hitting the pavement in one go.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Garncarska, bordering Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Teatr Bagatela tram stop or Krakow Glowny railway station, short walk
trees.notes: Three trunks from one base, girths 275cm, 203cm and 175cm, and the 1968 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.1067, gid 71989). girth_cm records the largest stem, not a single trunk. NO age given: no reliable species-appropriate growth factor exists for Ginkgo biloba, so an estimate would be a mismatched proxy rather than a derivation. The page asks readers for a planting record.

best_time.label: November, when the crown turns butter gold and drops almost all at once

trees.name: The Bartoszewski Square Oak
trees.age_estimate: estimated 140 to 210 years, from its girth

location.address: Skwer im. prof. Wladyslawa Bartoszewskiego (junction of ul. Basztowa, ul. Asnyka, ul. Garbarska and ul. Dunajewskiego), Krakow

trees.story:
The oak was on the register ten years before the square had a name. Krakow protected it in 2008. The city council voted on 10 October 2018 to name the ground around it after Wladyslaw Bartoszewski, a Home Army member who survived Auschwitz, was honoured as Righteous Among the Nations and later served as Poland's foreign minister. It is his square, not his oak. Nothing in the record links the tree to the man beyond the address, and the dates rule out the tidier story.

It is an odd oak in its own right. This is a columnar cultivar of the pedunculate oak, which grows narrow and upright instead of spreading, closer in outline to a poplar than to the wide-crowned oaks most people picture when they hear the word. The trunk is 288 centimetres around, standing where four streets meet at the northern edge of Planty.

Its age is calculated, not recorded. That girth gives about 92 centimetres of diameter, and the published factor for the white oak group returns roughly 180 years. Take the range, 140 to 210, and take it loosely: nobody has documented how fast a columnar cultivar thickens compared with an ordinary oak, which is uncertainty stacked on top of uncertainty.
trees.access: Free, public square, open at all hours
trees.transport: Poczta Glowna or Dworzec Glowny tram stops, short walk
trees.notes: Girth 288cm and the 2008 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.945, gid 72127). The square was named for Wladyslaw Bartoszewski by council vote on 10 October 2018, a decade after the tree's designation, per councillor Boguslaw Kosmider's site; no source connects the tree to Bartoszewski himself and the story does not. Age DERIVED from girth with the published white oak factor, band 140-210, widened further because a columnar cultivar's thickening rate against the straight species is undocumented.

trees.name: The Basztowa Turkish Hazel

location.address: Planty Krakowskie, near ul. Basztowa, Krakow

trees.story:
Turkish hazel is not the shrub its name suggests. Corylus colurna is a proper forest tree, native to southeast Europe and Asia Minor, capable of 25 metres and a neat conical crown, which is why cities plant it along streets when they want something tough and tidy. Krakow's protected list runs heavily to oaks, limes and planes, so a hazel on it is an oddity, and this one stands in Planty itself beside ul. Basztowa, close to the main station.

It grows as two stems from one base, 165 and 120 centimetres round. The 165 is the larger stem rather than a single trunk, which is worth stating plainly: the two figures do not add together, and a two-stemmed tree reads as bulkier than either measurement on its own. The city registered it in 2008.

Its age is not known. The growth-factor arithmetic used on the oaks and limes nearby needs a divisor matched to the species, and the only hazel figure in the standard tables is calibrated to common hazel, a multi-stemmed shrub with nothing like this tree's habit. Applying it would produce a number, not an estimate. If anyone holds a planting date for this corner of Planty, we would like to hear it.
trees.access: Free, public park (Planty), open at all hours
trees.transport: Dworzec Glowny (Krakow Glowny) tram/bus stops, short walk through Planty
trees.notes: Two trunks from one base, girths 165cm and 120cm, and the 2008 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.943, gid 72125). girth_cm records the larger stem, not a single trunk. NO age given: the only published hazel growth factor is calibrated to common hazel (Corylus avellana), a shrubby species with a different habit, so applying it to Corylus colurna would be a mismatched proxy. The page asks readers for a planting record.

trees.name: The Krowoderska Lime
trees.age_estimate: estimated 130 to 175 years, from its girth

location.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto / Krowodrza border, north of the Old Town

trees.story:
Four of the ages on this walk come off a tape measure rather than out of any record, and this is the only one where the arithmetic gets to use the tree's own species. The published growth factor for small-leaved lime is an exact match for what stands at ul. Krowoderska 16: a trunk 402 centimetres round, which converts to about 128 centimetres of diameter and returns roughly 150 years. Even then the honest form is a range, 130 to 175, because a growth factor describes an average lime rather than this one, and this one has spent its whole life in a street.

Poles have a longer relationship with the species than most. Lipa is the Polish name for it, and lipiec, the word for July, comes from the same root, because July is when the lime flowers and the tree fills with bees loud enough to hear from the pavement. Villages planted them at churches and crossroads for centuries.

This one has been protected since 1987 and is a city tree by contrast, on a working street north of the Old Town rather than in the park ring. It marks the far end of the Planty loop, about 1.2 kilometres from the ash on ul. Straszewskiego at the other extreme.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Krowoderska), open at all hours
trees.transport: Nowy Kleparz or Basztowa tram stops, short walk
trees.notes: Girth 402cm and the 1987 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.914, gid 72100). Age DERIVED from girth; the published growth factor for littleleaf linden is an exact species match, giving roughly 151 years, stated as 130-175. Not to be narrowed without a dendrochronological source.

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.name: The Studencka Plane
trees.age_estimate: estimated 90 to 165 years, from its girth

location.neighbourhood: Piasek, west of the Planty ring (Stare Miasto)

trees.story:
Krakow's biggest registered plane, on the Planty by the Philharmonic, measures 520 centimetres round. The one outside ul. Studencka 25 is a third smaller, 315 centimetres, and still made the city's natural monument register in 1997 on its own merits, a full street away from the Planty ring in the old Piasek district.

Its age is arithmetic rather than record. Working the girth through the growth factor already used for its bigger relative on the Planty, borrowed from American sycamore since no rate has been published for London plane itself, puts it somewhere between 90 and 165 years old. That is a wide bracket on purpose. Nobody has cored the trunk, and a tree growing between a road and a row of nineteenth century apartment blocks answers to the paving and pipes around it as much as to its own species.

London planes were planted through Krakow by the hundreds a century or more ago because almost nothing kills them: not compacted soil, not exhaust, not a hard prune. This one has outlasted whatever stood on Studencka before it, on a street that has changed its own name four times since 1893 while the tree kept growing. Free to walk up to, any hour.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Studencka), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre
trees.notes: Girth 315cm and the 1997 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.2972, gid 209479). Age DERIVED from girth using the same growth factor already applied to kra_005 (borrowed from American sycamore, the closest documented proxy for London plane); band not to be narrowed without a dendrochronological source.

trees.name: The Kossaka Square Ash
trees.age_estimate: estimated 130 to 190 years, from its girth
trees.story:
Plac Kossaka today is better known for parked cars and a kebab stand than for its trees, which is what makes the ash at number 4 easy to miss. It measures 321 centimetres around, entered onto Krakow's natural monument register in 1997, and stands a few streets from the city's other protected ash on ul. Straszewskiego, itself 375 centimetres and estimated at 150 to 220 years old by the same method.

Scaling this tree's girth against that already-published estimate, using the same borrowed growth factor (European ash has none of its own published, so the figure comes from green ash, its closest documented relative), puts the Kossaka tree at roughly 130 to 190 years. Narrower trunk, younger tree, same square kilometre of the city.

European ash is one of the commonest species in Poland, which is exactly why a trunk this thick stands out. The species has also had a hard three decades: a fungal dieback moving west since the 1990s has thinned ash populations across the continent, killing young and old trees indiscriminately. A veteran ash surviving that, on a square used mostly for parking, is a small piece of luck rather than a guarantee. Free and open to the street at any hour.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (Plac Kossaka), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre
trees.notes: Girth 321cm and the 1997 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.2977, gid 209489). Age DERIVED by scaling against kra_006 (same species, same register, same borrowed green-ash growth factor), not an independent calculation.

trees.name: The Batorego Oak and Ginkgo
trees.species: Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) and Ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba)
trees.story:
Two protected trees stand two doors apart on ul. Batorego, a pedunculate oak at number 14 and a ginkgo at number 12, both entered onto Krakow's natural monument register on the same day in 1997. The oak is the thicker of the two, 336 centimetres around; the ginkgo measures 305.

Neither has a documented age, and this is one case where guessing off the girth would mislead rather than help. Oak and ginkgo do not share a growth pattern with the ash and plane already published nearby, and no reliable published growth factor for either species in this climate was found this pass. What is verified is simpler and enough on its own: two long-lived species, planted close enough together to have been a deliberate pairing rather than a coincidence, both still standing on an ordinary residential street.

Ginkgo is the more unusual of the two. Native to China and unrelated to any other tree alive today, the species survived the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs, and six ginkgos close to the 1945 blast at Hiroshima resprouted from scorched trunks and still stand there. This one has had an easier life, on a Krakow pavement, free to see at any hour.
trees.access: Free, roadside trees on public ground (ul. Batorego), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre
trees.notes: Two register entries, oak (kodinspire .2978, gid 209491, girth 336cm) and ginkgo (kodinspire .2979, gid 209492, girth 305cm), roughly 20m apart at ul. Batorego 14 and 12 respectively per Polish Wikipedia's reproduction of the register. Shipped as one entry since only one coordinate point is verified for the pair and they read as one destination; location_precision reflects that, not a surveyed pin on either individual trunk. No age estimate attempted: no published growth factor found this pass for standard-form Quercus robur or Ginkgo biloba in this climate.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Sikorskiego Square Oak

location.neighbourhood: Piasek, west of the Old Town

trees.story:
Plac Sikorskiego's oak is the youngest addition to Krakow's register among the trees on this page, protected in 2007 rather than in the 1997 batch that covers most of the others. Its girth, 263 centimetres, is also the smallest of the pedunculate oaks the city protects near its centre, behind both the columnar oak on Skwer Bartoszewskiego and the Jagiellonian and Henryk oaks published elsewhere on this walk.

No age has been published for it, and running an ordinary pedunculate oak's girth through a growth factor table is a riskier bet than for species like ash or plane on this list. A standard-form oak's growth rate varies more with soil, light and pruning history than almost anything else here, and no comparably grown oak from the same register gives a safe baseline to scale from. Better to leave the number out than guess at one.

What is certain is the trunk itself, thick enough at 263 centimetres to be a genuine veteran by any reasonable account, standing on a square named for the Polish general and prime minister in exile Wladyslaw Sikorski, who died in a plane crash off Gibraltar in 1943. Free to see at any hour.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (Plac Sikorskiego), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre
trees.notes: Girth 263cm and the 2007 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.944, gid 72126). No age derived: kra_009, the only other published Krakow oak with a girth-based estimate, is a columnar cultivar (Quercus robur 'Fastigiata') with a different growth habit and is not a safe proxy for a standard-form oak.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Tarlowska Lime
trees.age_estimate: estimated 85 to 115 years, from its girth

location.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto, near the Planty ring

trees.story:
Krakow already protects one small-leaved lime on this page, a 402 centimetre trunk on ul. Krowoderska whose age comes out at 130 to 175 years by the species' own published growth factor, an unusually exact match between the tape measure and the science. The lime on ul. Tarlowska is the smaller of the city's two, 259 centimetres round, entered onto the register in 2004, seventeen years after most of the trees on this walk.

Running the same growth factor against this thinner trunk gives a range of roughly 85 to 115 years, which would put its planting somewhere in the interwar years or just after, plausible for a street lime on a residential road rebuilt more than once since. As with its bigger relative, the number is arithmetic rather than record: nobody has cored it, and the bracket stays wide on purpose.

Small-leaved lime was the tree cities across Central Europe reached for through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, tolerant of pollution, easy to pollard, long-lived enough to still be standing when the street around it has changed shape several times over. This one is free to walk up to on ul. Tarlowska at any hour.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Tarlowska), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Planty ring / Stare Miasto centre
trees.notes: Girth 259cm and the 2004 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.911, gid 72098). Age DERIVED by scaling against kra_007 (same species, same register, same published small-leaved lime growth factor).

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.name: The Sw. Jana Tree of Heaven

location.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto (Old Town core, between the Main Square and the Planty)

trees.story:
Ulica Swietego Jana runs from the Main Square to the Planty, one of the most walked streets in the Old Town, and the tree registered at number 30 is a species most European cities spend money trying to remove. Ailanthus altissima, tree of heaven, seeds into any crack in the pavement, sends up suckers under paving stones and shades out whatever grew there first, fast enough to reach a serious size within a single lifetime. Krakow protects this one anyway, entered onto the natural monument register in 1997 for a trunk 292 centimetres around.

That speed is exactly why no age is published here. A growth factor that works for an oak or a lime tells you nothing about a tree that can add a metre of height in a good year. Dublin's own registered tree of heaven carries an official estimate of 120 to 165 years that the species' own growth pattern argues should be closer to 70 or 100. Rather than repeat that kind of guess, this page states the girth and leaves the age open.

What is not in doubt is the tree itself, standing on one of Krakow's busiest historic streets, growing well before anyone thought to protect it.
trees.access: Free, roadside tree on public ground (ul. Swietego Jana), open at all hours
trees.transport: Short walk from the Main Square, Stare Miasto
trees.notes: Girth 292cm and the 1997 designation from Krakow's registry list as reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, cross-checked against GDOS/CRFOP (PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1261011.992, gid 72171). No age estimate: Ailanthus altissima's growth rate is too fast and site-dependent for a girth-based band to be honest, per the same caution already published on data/species/tree-of-heaven.json (Dublin comparison).

trees.name: The Franciszkanska Ginkgo

location.neighbourhood: Stare Miasto (Old Town), beside the Franciscan church

trees.access: Free. Stands on ul. Franciszkańska in the Old Town, beside the Church of the Franciscans (kościół oo. Franciszkanów); publicly visible and reachable from the street at all times.
trees.transport: Filharmonia tram stop, about 3 minutes' walk.
trees.story:
Nobody has measured this ginkgo's age, but its trunk gives away that it is old enough to fruit, a milestone the species does not reach for about forty years. It grows on ul. Franciszkanska beside the Church of the Franciscans in the Old Town, a two hundred and fifty eight centimetre trunk standing where monks have kept a garden for centuries.

Poland's national register of natural monuments lists the tree's protection as dating from 1998; the city's own official list, reproduced on Polish Wikipedia, gives 1997 for this tree and several others nearby, a discrepancy that most likely traces to a province-wide reconfirmation regulation rather than a disagreement about the tree itself. Both dates are recorded here rather than picked between.

Ginkgo biloba survived in cultivation around temple grounds in East Asia for centuries before European gardens took it up, and it tends to end up beside old religious buildings for the same reason it did here: nobody with authority over sacred ground had reason to cut down something that was simply doing well. No age has been established for this specimen. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The Powroznicza Red Oak

location.neighbourhood: Podgórze, in the garden of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (district public library)

trees.access: Free. Stands in the grounds of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (Podgórze District Public Library) at ul. Powroźnicza 2, a public institution housed in a late-19th-century villa; reachable during the library's opening hours.
trees.transport: In Podgórze, roughly a 10-minute walk from Rynek Podgórski; bus routes serving nearby ul. Kalwaryjska and Rynek Podgórski are the closest public transport.
trees.story:
Krakow's monumental trees are almost all native oaks and limes, which makes this one an outlier twice over: a Northern Red Oak, a North American species, growing in the garden of a public library. The building itself has its own history worth knowing before the tree. Built as a villa in the late 1880s and once purchased for the painter Jan Matejko's daughter Beata, it has served as Podgorze district's public library since 1988, which is what keeps its garden open rather than walled off as someone's private grounds.

The oak's trunk measures three metres fourteen around, big enough that Poland's national register protects it as a natural monument, though the register itself carries no age. Its protection date is recorded two ways, 1987 in the national database and 1997 in the city's own list, likely the gap between an original designation and a later province-wide reconfirmation rather than a real dispute.

A honey locust stands twelve metres away in the same garden, registered alongside it under the same library grounds. No age has been established for either, and an introduced ornamental species like this one has no reliable local growth rate to estimate from. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The Powroznicza Honey Locust

location.neighbourhood: Podgórze, in the garden of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (district public library)

trees.access: Free. Stands in the grounds of the Podgórska Biblioteka Publiczna (Podgórze District Public Library) at ul. Powroźnicza 2, a public institution housed in a late-19th-century villa; reachable during the library's opening hours.
trees.transport: In Podgórze, roughly a 10-minute walk from Rynek Podgórski; bus routes serving nearby ul. Kalwaryjska and Rynek Podgórski are the closest public transport.
trees.story:
Twelve metres from the library's red oak stands its quieter neighbour, a honey locust with a trunk two metres twenty three around, one of relatively few of its species protected anywhere in Krakow as a natural monument. Both trees share the same garden, the grounds of the Podgorze district public library, a villa built in the 1880s that has kept its grounds open to the public since it became a library in 1988.

Gleditsia triacanthos is a North American species, armed in the wild with vicious branching thorns that cultivated street and garden specimens are usually bred without, and it took to European ornamental planting in the nineteenth century the way its oak neighbour did. Poland's national register protects it on species and location alone, with no girth or age recorded there; the city's own official list adds the measurement.

The two protection dates disagree by a decade, 1987 nationally against 1997 in the city record, in the same pattern as its neighbour and several other Krakow trees this pass checked, most likely a province wide reconfirmation rather than two different true dates. No age has been established. If you know one, tell us.

trees.name: The Kosciuszki Silver Lime
trees.access: Free. Stands on ul. Kościuszki in Krowodrza, visible and reachable from the public street.
trees.transport: Bus routes 134 and 502 run along ul. Kościuszki.
trees.story:
Krakow already has one small leaved lime on this list whose age comes from an unusually exact match between a tape measure and the published science: the Krowoderska Lime, four hundred and two centimetres round, dated to 130 to 175 years by the species' own documented growth rate. This tree, on the same street, is a different species entirely, a silver lime, and its own trunk has grown even thicker: four hundred and twenty four centimetres.

No document records when it was planted, so its age here is derived rather than measured: applying the growth rate this city's own lime data already established, widened to allow for the difference between species, puts it at roughly 130 to 190 years old. That is an estimate from girth, not a planting record, and the wide band is the honest shape of that kind of arithmetic.

Poland's national register dates its protection to 1975; the city's own list gives 1997, the same reconfirmation-year pattern seen elsewhere on this page. It stands on ul. Kosciuszki in Krowodrza, visible from the public street, served by two city bus routes.

trees.name: The Daszynskiego Lime
trees.access: Free. Stands on Aleja Ignacego Daszyńskiego, a public avenue in Śródmieście; visible and reachable from the street at all times.
trees.transport: Tram lines 1, 10, 20, 24, 50 and 52 run along Aleja Daszyńskiego; the tree is a short walk from house number 13.
trees.story:
This lime is the youngest of three different Tilia species this page now protects, and the arithmetic that ages it borrows from the other two. Krakow's own small leaved limes gave a documented growth rate for this climate; applied to this tree's two hundred and eighty four centimetre trunk, with room left for the uncertainty of crossing species, it comes out at roughly 85 to 130 years. That is an estimate built from girth, not a planting date, and the width of the range is the honest price of that method.

Unlike its neighbours on this page, this large leaved lime carries an exact and recent paper trail: Krakow's city council protected it by name in a resolution dated 16 December 2015, entered into the national register three weeks later. No thirty year gap between two dates here, just the ordinary lag between a vote and its paperwork.

It grows on Aleja Daszynskiego in Srodmiescie, a wide tram lined avenue rather than a park, doing the quiet work street trees do: six tram lines run past it, and Wikimedia Commons already has a photograph of it standing there among the traffic.

trees.name: The Bednarski Park Black Walnut

location.address: Park im. Wojciecha Bednarskiego, Podgorze, Krakow

trees.access: Free, open public park (Zarzad Zieleni Miejskiej), entrances on ul. Parkowa and ul. Zamoyskiego near Plac Niepodleglosci
trees.transport: Podgorze tram stops (Rondo Matecznego / Plac Bohaterow Getta area), roughly 10-15 min walk uphill into the park
trees.story:
Krakow's register of natural monuments holds exactly one black walnut, and this is it. The city recorded 298 centimetres of trunk when it granted the tree protection in February 2017.

The species belongs to the river valleys of eastern North America, not to a Polish hillside, and it is here because the park around it was built to show things off. Park Bednarskiego was laid out inside a worked-out limestone quarry from the 1890s, its terraces planted with what the city had little of: tulip tree, tree of heaven, this walnut. The garden section it stands in is called Szkola Twardowskiego, the school of Twardowski, after the sorcerer whose workshop local legend placed in the quarry basin.

Black walnut makes its case in autumn. The fruit comes down in green husks the size of tennis balls, and the pulp inside stains hands, gloves and paving a brown that does not wash off.

The whole park closed for rebuilding in January 2022 and reopened on 27 April 2023, the work written up as keeping the existing old growth standing. This tree came through it.

Nobody has recorded its age. The park was planted in more than one campaign and no source ties this trunk to any of them. If you know when it went in, tell us.

best_time.label: late September into October, when the green husks come down and stain everything they touch

trees.name: The Bednarski Park Larch

location.address: Park im. Wojciecha Bednarskiego, Podgorze, Krakow

trees.access: Free, open public park (Zarzad Zieleni Miejskiej), entrances on ul. Parkowa and ul. Zamoyskiego near Plac Niepodleglosci
trees.transport: Podgorze tram stops (Rondo Matecznego / Plac Bohaterow Getta area), roughly 10-15 min walk uphill into the park
trees.story:
The slope this larch grows on was fenced, guarded and shut to the public for roughly half a century. Park Bednarskiego planted its western side as woodland between 1902 and 1909, named the section Zalesienie, and then kept people out of it with high fines for trespassing. It opened to walkers only in the 1950s, decades after the rest of the park was in daily use.

The tree is also the only European larch on Krakow's list of natural monuments. The city recorded 223 centimetres of trunk when it protected the tree in February 2017, in the same council resolution that covered three of its neighbours in this park.

Larch is the conifer that does not stay green. Soft needles in little bunches, fresh green in April, gold through late October, and by December nothing at all: a bare grey frame standing among evergreens that kept theirs. Almost nothing else in a European park does that, and it is the reason to come here in November rather than in July.

No age is recorded for it anywhere, and the park's own planting history is not specific enough to supply one honestly. If you know this tree's story, we would like to hear it. The park closed for a full rebuild in 2022 and reopened in April 2023 with its old growth kept in place, so what you walk up to is the tree the register measured.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn gold and then drop

trees.name: The Bednarski Park Ash

location.address: Park im. Wojciecha Bednarskiego, Podgorze, Krakow

trees.access: Free, open public park (Zarzad Zieleni Miejskiej), entrances on ul. Parkowa and ul. Zamoyskiego near Plac Niepodleglosci
trees.transport: Podgorze tram stops (Rondo Matecznego / Plac Bohaterow Getta area), roughly 10-15 min walk uphill into the park
trees.story:
Krakow protects three European ashes, and this is the only one that does not grow out of a pavement. The other two stand on ul. Straszewskiego and on Plac Kossaka, thicker trunks but boxed in by kerbs and parked cars. This one has a park around it.

It measures 278 centimetres round, the figure the city entered when it added the tree to the register in February 2017. Ash is the species that gives Park Bednarskiego its shape: jesiony line the Aleja Okrezna, the circular promenade that carries walkers around the old quarry basin, and this is the trunk the register picked out of the row.

The ground is worth knowing about before you get there. The park is a worked-out limestone quarry turned into a public garden from the 1890s, terraced where the stone had been cut away, so everything growing here is standing on an industrial site that was given back. The city rebuilt the park between January 2022 and April 2023 and wrote the old trees into the specification, which is why the promenade still has its ash.

No record gives this tree an age, and the park's history is not precise enough to settle it without guessing. A tape measure round the trunk at chest height would get us closer than any document we have found. If you have one, tell us what it says.

trees.name: The Bednarski Park Sycamore Maple

location.address: Park im. Wojciecha Bednarskiego, Podgorze, Krakow

trees.access: Free, open public park (Zarzad Zieleni Miejskiej), entrances on ul. Parkowa and ul. Zamoyskiego near Plac Niepodleglosci
trees.transport: Podgorze tram stops (Rondo Matecznego / Plac Bohaterow Getta area), roughly 10-15 min walk uphill into the park
trees.story:
The city's register carries this maple under two numbers, 204 centimetres and 191, because it has two trunks rather than one. That is the register being careful, and it is also the easiest way to find the tree: among the maples on this slope, look for the one going up as a pair.

Sycamore is a mountain species, the maple of the Carpathians and the Alps, and it makes timber size on thin stony ground where most broadleaves give up. Park Bednarskiego, cut into a limestone quarry above Podgorze and planted from the 1890s, is that kind of ground. Three maple species grow here and this is the klon jawor, the one whose bark flakes off in plates as it ages, leaving the trunk mottled like a plane tree.

It was protected in February 2017, one of four trees in this single garden that Krakow put on the natural monument register in one council resolution, alongside a black walnut, a European larch and an ash. Four monuments inside one park, which is why this hillside is worth an afternoon rather than a detour.

Nobody has dated it, and no source says whether it was planted here or seeded itself, which sycamore does readily. If you know more about this one, tell us.

trees.name: The Kosciuszki Norway Maple
trees.access: Free, street tree on public ground (ul. Kosciuszki), visible and reachable at all times
trees.transport: Same street as the already-published Kosciuszki Silver Lime (kra_020), about 115m away; same tram/bus stops on ul. Kosciuszki
trees.story:
Norway maple is the tree Krakow plants when it simply needs a tree. It lines streets all over the city, which is what makes a protected one strange: in 2020 the council entered this specimen at ul. Kosciuszki 18 on the register of natural monuments, at 210 centimetres round.

The girth is the whole case. Street maples are pruned back, hemmed in under paving and usually replaced long before they thicken, so a trunk over two metres round on an open pavement is not what the species normally manages in a city.

It is also the second monument on this stretch of road. The Kosciuszki Silver Lime, twice as thick at 424 centimetres, stands about 115 metres along the same street, so the two are one short walk rather than two separate trips.

April is the moment worth turning up for. Norway maple flowers before it leafs, and the bare crown fills with clusters of acid yellow-green that read, on a grey Krakow street, as the first colour of the year. A broken leaf stalk bleeds milky white, which is how the species is told from the sycamore it otherwise resembles.

No age is on record. The register is interested in the measurement rather than the year, and nobody has published a figure. If you know when this one went in, tell us.

best_time.label: April, when it flowers before it leafs and the bare crown turns acid yellow-green
